claims.claim: A. fumigatus HapX undergoes post-translational modifications (ubiquitination, sumoylation, and phosphorylation) during iron-replete conditions.
claims.source: It has to be mentioned that recent studies in A. fumigatus obtained similar observations. Similar to Hap43, the A. fumigatus homologue HapX also undergoes post-translational modifications (ubiquitination, sumoylation, and phosphorylation) during iron-replete conditions and these post-translational regulations are important to control iron homeostasis in A. fumigatus (López-Berges et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to López-Berges et al., 2021.

claims.claim: A. fumigatus HapX exhibits inverse regulatory activities by mediating repression or activation of vacuolar iron storage depending on iron availability.
claims.source: Moreover, A. fumigatus HapX exhibits inverse regulatory activities by mediating repression or activation of vacuolar iron storage depending on the ambient iron availability, suggesting that HapX appears to be important for regulating both iron resistance and adaptation to iron starvation (Gsaller et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gsaller et al., 2014.

claims.claim: C. albicans Hap43 plays only a minor role in mediating adaptation to iron excess.
claims.source: Interestingly, C. albicans Hap43, in stark contrast to HapX of A. fumigatus, appears to play only a minor role in mediating the adaption to iron excess, although this factor did act positively for the activation of iron uptake genes during iron starvation (Skrahina et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Skrahina et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Replacement of all 29 S/T residues abolished the upward shift (phosphorylation) of Hap43-Myc band induced by high iron.
claims.source: An immunoblot with cell lysates from both WT (Hap43-Myc/hap43Δ) and HAP43 mutant-29 (Hap43m29-Myc/hap43Δ) clearly revealed that the replacement of all 29S/T residues abolished the upward shift (phosphorylation) of Hap43-Myc band induced by high iron and as a result significantly increased the steady level of Hap43 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The region within residues 330–400 of Hap43 harbors the signal contributing to phosphorylation-dependent degradation.
claims.source: Among them, Hap43 truncating mutations (Δ400 and Δ504) give rise to almost similar levels as the full length of WT, whereas the mutation (Δ330) results in a suddenly dramatic increase of Hap43 level. These results strongly suggest that the region within residues 330–400 harbors the signal contributing the phosphorylation-dependent degradation of Hap43.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on truncation mutants.

claims.claim: Deletion of 36 amino acid residues (346–381 aa) leads to increased level of truncated Hap43 and abrogated high iron-induced protein degradation.
claims.source: Similar to the phenotypes observed in the HAP43 mutant, deletion of the 36 amino acid residues also leads to increased level of the truncated form of Hap43 (Figure 4E) and abrogated the high iron-induced protein degradation (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claims.claim: The HAP43m4 mutant exhibited significantly higher level of Hap43 proteins than WT under high iron conditions.
claims.source: Consistently, we found that under high iron conditions, the mutant exhibited significantly higher level of Hap43 proteins than that of the wild type (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: ROS levels were moderately elevated in C. albicans cells after incubation in YPD medium.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5A and B, ROS levels were moderately elevated in C. albicans cells after incubation in YPD medium, whereas massive increase was observed in medium supplemented with FeCl3, to a level comparable to that observed in medium with H2O2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: Massive increase in ROS was observed in medium supplemented with FeCl3.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5A and B, ROS levels were moderately elevated in C. albicans cells after incubation in YPD medium, whereas massive increase was observed in medium supplemented with FeCl3, to a level comparable to that observed in medium with H2O2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: Iron-induced ROS production via Fenton reaction could be prevented by treating cells with NAC.
claims.source: As controls, iron-induced ROS production via Fenton reaction could be prevented by treating the cells with the antioxidant N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: High levels of iron are sufficient to significantly enhance ROS production in C. albicans.
claims.source: These data clearly indicated that high levels of iron are sufficient to significantly enhanced ROS production in C. albicans.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ROS production.

claims.claim: Iron-triggered degradation of Hap43 could be inhibited by treating cells with NAC.
claims.source: More importantly, we observed that iron-triggered degradation of Hap43 could be inhibited by treating the cells with NAC (Figure 5C) and treatment of C. albicans cells with menadione, an inducer of endogenous ROS, leads to the reduction of the Hap43 protein level (Figure 5D), supporting the proposition that the promotion of iron-induced generation of ROS may account for the SSN3-dependent ubiquitination and phosphorylation-dependent degradation of Hap43.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Treatment of C. albicans cells with menadione leads to reduction of Hap43 protein level.
claims.source: More importantly, we observed that iron-triggered degradation of Hap43 could be inhibited by treating the cells with NAC (Figure 5C) and treatment of C. albicans cells with menadione, an inducer of endogenous ROS, leads to the reduction of the Hap43 protein level (Figure 5D), supporting the proposition that the promotion of iron-induced generation of ROS may account for the SSN3-dependent ubiquitination and phosphorylation-dependent degradation of Hap43.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Deletion of HAP43 showed remarkable resistance to H2O2.
claims.source: Compared to the WT, deletion of HAP43 showed remarkable resistance to H2O2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that loss of Hap43 promotes cell survival under oxidative stress.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Abolishment of Hap43 phosphorylation in mutants showed significantly greater sensitivity to oxidative stress compared to WT.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also found that compared to the WT (Hap43-Myc/hap43Δ), abolishment of Hap43 phosphorylation in each of the three mutants generated above, including the Hap43 truncation mutant (Hap43tr-Myc/hap43Δ), HAP43 mutant-29 (Hap43m29-Myc/hap43Δ), or HAP43 mutant-4 (Hap43m4-Myc/hap43Δ), showed significantly greater sensitivity to oxidative stress (Figure 5E–G), arguing that the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of Hap43 after phosphorylation contributes to the protection against ROS-induced cytotoxicity.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claims.claim: HAP43 mutant-29, Hap43 truncation, and HAP43 mutant-4 mutants could be outcompeted by WT strain in mouse GI tract.
claims.source: This notion was further supported by the in vivo evidence that the HAP43 mutant-29, Hap43 truncation, and HAP43 mutant-4 mutants could be outcompeted by the WT strain when cells stably colonize in mouse GI tract (Figure 5H–J).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5H–J.

claims.claim: Iron-induced Hap43 phosphorylation and degradation protect C. albicans from ROS toxicity and promote survival in GI tract.
claims.source: Taken together, our data highly suggest that iron-induced Hap43 phosphorylation, followed by ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation, acts to protect C. albicans from ROS toxicity and thus promote its survival in GI tract, a niche normally considered as an iron-replete environment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Unphosphorylated forms of Hap43 (Hap43tr, Hap43m29, and Hap43m4) localized to the nucleus under iron-replete conditions.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, WT Hap43 localized to the cytoplasm, while unphosphorylated form of Hap43 (Hap43tr, Hap43m29, and Hap43m4) localized to the nucleus, suggesting that abolishing the phosphorylation-dependent modification resulted in relocation of Hap43 from cytoplasm to nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The mutated or truncated Hap43 (Hap43tr or Hap43m29) significantly enriched in the promoter regions of antioxidant genes.
claims.source: As expected, the mutated or truncated Hap43 (Hap43tr or Hap43m29) significantly enriched in the promoter regions of the four target antioxidant genes (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), which suggested a direct regulation of ROS detoxification in C. albicans by post-translational modification of Hap43.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Hap43 significantly repressed the expression of CAT1 and SOD2 in Hap43tr, Hap43m29, and Hap43m4 strains.
claims.source: Indeed, when the expression levels of these four antioxidant genes were examined by qPCR, we found that upon binding to the promoters directly, Hap43 significantly repressed the expression of CAT1 and SOD2 in Hap43tr, Hap43m29, and Hap43m4 strains (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Iron-induced post-translational modification of Hap43 results in de-repression of antioxidant genes (e.g., CAT1 and SOD2).
claims.source: Taken together, our data proposed a model (Figure 7) that the iron-induced post-translational modification of Hap43, including cytoplasmic localization, Ssn3-dependent phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and proteasomal degradation, results in the de-repression of antioxidant genes (e.g. CAT1 and SOD2), an event that is most effective in lowering cytotoxicity induced by oxidative stress and promotes C. albicans commensalism in GI tract.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data, as shown in Figure 7.

results.result: High-iron diet (HFD) increases iron levels and ROS production in mouse colon. Mice fed HFD (400 mg/kg Fe) showed significantly increased colonic iron levels (C32), ROS production measured by DHE fluorescence (C33), DUOX2 mRNA expression (C34), and H2O2 levels (C35) compared to normal-iron diet (NFD, 180 mg/kg Fe) mice, which showed minimal ROS (C31). The authors conclude HFD sustains persistent ROS exposure in the gut (C36).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 provide converging experimental evidence from multiple independent assays (Prussian blue staining, DHE fluorescence, qRT-PCR, H2O2 measurement) demonstrating that HFD increases both iron and ROS in mouse colon. The experimental design (C29) is appropriate with proper controls (NFD vs HFD), and statistical significance is reported. The conclusion (C36) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Deletion of HAP43 enhances C. albicans colonization fitness in HFD-fed mice. HFD increased fungal loads in mouse feces (C37), and the hap43Δ/Δ mutant significantly outcompeted wild-type C. albicans in competitive colonization assays in HFD-fed mice (C38). Treatment with antioxidant NAC reduced the competitive advantage of the hap43Δ/Δ mutant (C39).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 provide direct experimental evidence using competitive colonization assays with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The NAC rescue experiment (C39) supports the mechanistic link to ROS. However, C30 shows no difference in NFD-fed mice, which is critical context suggesting the phenotype is HFD-specific. The convergence of these results strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: High iron induces rapid phosphorylation of Hap43. Hap43 protein levels and electrophoretic mobility change under iron-replete versus iron-depleted conditions (C40-C42). Lambda phosphatase treatment reversed the mobility shift (C43), demonstrating the shift is due to phosphorylation (C44).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 provide direct biochemical evidence from immunoblotting and phosphatase treatment experiments. The lambda phosphatase experiment (C43) is the critical control that definitively establishes phosphorylation as the mechanism for the mobility shift. The rapid kinetics (2 min, C42) support iron-responsive regulation. The conclusion (C44) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: Ssn3 kinase mediates Hap43 phosphorylation. The mobility shift of Hap43 under iron-replete conditions was abolished in ssn3Δ/Δ mutant and kinase-dead Ssn3D325A strain (C45), supporting Ssn3's role in Hap43 phosphorylation (C46). Co-immunoprecipitation showed Hap43-Myc interacts with Ssn3-TAP under both iron conditions (C47).
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C47 provide genetic and biochemical evidence for Ssn3-Hap43 interaction and Ssn3's role in phosphorylation. The use of both knockout and kinase-dead mutants strengthens the conclusion. The co-IP experiment (C47) demonstrates physical interaction. Together, these data strongly support that Ssn3 phosphorylates Hap43.

results.result: Ssn3-mediated phosphorylation regulates Hap43 subcellular localization and protein stability. Under iron-replete conditions, Hap43 localizes to cytoplasm in WT but partially to nucleus in ssn3Δ/Δ mutant (C49-C50), while localization is nuclear in both strains under iron-depleted conditions (C48). Deletion of SSN3 does not affect HAP43 mRNA levels (C51) but stabilizes Hap43 protein (C52-C53), indicating post-translational regulation of protein stability by Ssn3 (C54).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 provide microscopy and fractionation data showing Ssn3-dependent localization changes. Claims C51-C53 demonstrate that Ssn3 affects protein stability without changing mRNA levels, using appropriate promoter shut-off experiments. The convergence of localization and stability data strongly supports the conclusion (C54) that Ssn3 regulates Hap43 post-translationally.

results.result: Hap43 is degraded through the proteasomal pathway under high iron conditions. Proteasome inhibitor MG132 significantly increased Hap43 protein levels (C55), while lysosome inhibitor chloroquine had no effect (C56), demonstrating proteasomal degradation (C57).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 provide direct pharmacological evidence using specific inhibitors for proteasome and lysosome pathways. The differential effects of MG132 (positive) versus chloroquine (negative) clearly distinguish the degradation pathway. The use of erg6Δ mutant to enhance drug permeability is appropriate. The conclusion (C57) is well-supported.

results.result: Ssn3-mediated phosphorylation promotes Hap43 ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Only phosphorylated Hap43 (WT) but not unphosphorylated Hap43 (ssn3Δ/Δ) bound ubiquitin (C58). TAP-tagged Hap43 showed K48-linked polyubiquitination (C59), the canonical signal for proteasomal degradation. Together, these data support that Ssn3-mediated phosphorylation promotes ubiquitin-proteasome pathway degradation of Hap43 (C60).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 provide direct biochemical evidence from immunoprecipitation experiments. The use of K48-linkage-specific antibodies (C59) is critical for establishing the proteasomal degradation signal. The genetic comparison (WT vs ssn3Δ/Δ, C58) demonstrates phosphorylation-dependence. The conclusion (C60) integrates multiple lines of evidence and is well-supported.

results.result: Multiple serine/threonine residues in Hap43 are required for phosphorylation-dependent degradation. Replacement of all 29 predicted S/T residues abolished phosphorylation and increased Hap43 protein levels (C64). Truncation analysis identified residues 330-400 as critical for degradation (C65). Deletion of residues 346-381 prevented phosphorylation and degradation (C66). Mutation of four specific residues (S337/S355/S369/T381) also increased Hap43 levels (C67).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 provide systematic mutagenesis data identifying phosphorylation sites. The approach progresses logically from comprehensive mutation (29 sites) to domain mapping (truncations) to specific residues (4 sites). Multiple independent mutants show consistent phenotypes (increased protein levels, abolished phosphorylation). The convergence of these approaches strongly supports the identification of critical phosphorylation sites.

results.result: High iron levels significantly enhance ROS production in C. albicans. ROS levels were moderately elevated in YPD medium (C68) but massively increased with FeCl3 supplementation (C69), comparable to H2O2 treatment. NAC treatment prevented iron-induced ROS (C70), confirming iron-mediated ROS generation via Fenton reaction (C71).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 provide direct experimental evidence using fluorometric ROS detection with appropriate controls (YPD, FeCl3, H2O2, NAC). The NAC rescue (C70) is critical for establishing the Fenton reaction mechanism. The conclusion (C71) is well-supported by the data and consistent with established iron chemistry.

results.result: Hap43 phosphorylation and degradation protect C. albicans from ROS toxicity and promote GI colonization. NAC inhibited iron-triggered Hap43 degradation (C72), while ROS inducer menadione reduced Hap43 levels (C73), linking ROS to Hap43 degradation. Deletion of HAP43 conferred H2O2 resistance (C74), but preventing Hap43 phosphorylation (mutants Hap43tr, Hap43m29, Hap43m4) increased oxidative stress sensitivity (C75) and reduced colonization fitness in vivo (C76). Together, these data support that iron-induced Hap43 phosphorylation and degradation protect against ROS and promote GI survival (C77).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 provide converging evidence from pharmacological (NAC, menadione), genetic (deletion, phosphorylation mutants), and in vivo (colonization) experiments. The apparent paradox (deletion increases resistance, C74, but preventing phosphorylation increases sensitivity, C75) is resolved by understanding that complete loss versus stabilization have different effects. The in vivo validation (C76) is critical. The conclusion (C77) integrates multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Iron-induced phosphorylation and degradation of Hap43 leads to de-repression of antioxidant genes. Unphosphorylated Hap43 mutants (Hap43tr, Hap43m29, Hap43m4) localized to the nucleus under iron-replete conditions (C78), enriched at promoters of antioxidant genes (C79), and repressed CAT1 and SOD2 expression (C80). The model proposes that iron-induced Hap43 modification results in de-repression of antioxidant genes, reducing ROS toxicity and promoting commensalism (C81).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 provide direct evidence from microscopy, ChIP-qPCR, and gene expression analysis. The logic is clear: preventing phosphorylation causes nuclear localization, DNA binding, and gene repression, implying that normal phosphorylation prevents these events and allows gene expression. The model (C81) is well-supported by the data, though some genes (TRR1, GSH1) show inconsistent results, suggesting additional regulatory complexity.

results.result: Iron is essential but toxic at high levels through ROS production. Iron is crucial for living cells (C1, C7) and acts as an enzyme cofactor in electron transfer and catalysis (C8). However, excess iron is toxic through ROS generation via Haber-Weiss/Fenton reaction (C2, C9).
results.evaluation: These claims represent well-established scientific knowledge supported by citations and general knowledge. They provide essential background context for the study but are not novel findings. The claims are accurate and appropriately cited.

results.result: The mammalian gut is an iron-rich environment where excess iron aggravates oxidative stress. The gut contains high levels of unabsorbed dietary iron (C10, C11), which likely aggravates oxidative stress (C12) and restricts microbial growth through ROS-induced cellular toxicity (C13).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are supported by appropriate citations. Claim C12 is an inference that is reasonable given the cited data. Claim C13 is supported by citations. These claims provide important background context establishing the biological relevance of the study but are not novel findings from this work.

results.result: Microbes have evolved mechanisms to manage iron toxicity. Bacteria like E. coli and S. typhimurium use iron efflux systems (C14), while fungi use vacuolar and siderophore-mediated iron storage (C15) to prevent iron-induced ROS formation.
results.evaluation: Both claims are supported by appropriate citations and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide relevant background context for understanding microbial iron homeostasis strategies but are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: C. albicans iron homeostasis is regulated by Sfu1, Sef1, and Hap43. C. albicans is both a pathogen and commensal (C16-C17). Iron regulation involves three transcription factors: Sfu1 downregulates iron acquisition genes (C19), Sef1 activates iron uptake genes in low iron (C20), and Hap43 represses Sfu1 in low iron and is required for virulence (C21, C27). About 16% of C. albicans genes are Hap43-regulated, many involved in oxidative stress and iron metabolism (C28).
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by citations to previous work, primarily by the same authors (Chen et al., 2011). They provide essential background on the iron regulatory circuit and Hap43's known functions, establishing the foundation for the current study's novel findings. The claims accurately represent prior knowledge.

results.result: The CCAAT-binding factor is a conserved transcription factor complex. In mammals, NF-YA/B/C form the NF-Y complex (C22-C23). In S. cerevisiae, Hap2/3/4/5 form the HAP complex (C24-C25). Hap4 is fungal-specific and its homologs regulate iron responses (C26).
results.evaluation: These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and represent established knowledge about CCAAT-binding transcription factor complexes across eukaryotes. They provide important evolutionary and mechanistic context but are not novel findings.

results.result: Comparison of Hap43 regulation with A. fumigatus HapX. A. fumigatus HapX undergoes similar post-translational modifications (C61) and has dual regulatory roles in iron storage (C62), while C. albicans Hap43 plays a minor role in iron excess adaptation (C63).
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by appropriate citations and provide comparative context with related fungi. They help position the current findings within the broader fungal biology literature. The comparison is accurate based on the cited work.

results.result: High iron triggers post-translational modifications and degradation of Hap43, leading to de-repression of antioxidant genes and ROS detoxification. This mechanism allows Hap43 to function as a negative regulator of oxidative stress adaptation for gut colonization.
results.evaluation: These are summary claims from the abstract that integrate the major findings. They are well-supported by the detailed experimental evidence in claims C40-C81. Claims C4-C5 accurately summarize the mechanistic findings, and C6 appropriately states the biological significance. These represent the core conclusions of the paper.
